item.title: Why We Invested: System
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
At Courtside, the investments we’re most excited about tend to arrive the same way: a category we’ve been quietly studying for years suddenly collides with a catalyst we didn’t control.

This has certainly been true for us in consumer health and wellness, where we’ve spent an outsized amount of time (and capital) from Fund IV. We’ve been most interested in consumers taking health into their own hands, showing a seemingly unhindered willingness to spend out of pocket on solutions that promise a higher quality and duration of life.

Health and wellness has been on an upward trend categorically since our early days a decade ago when we launched Courtside Ventures, leading us to early investments in pain management (Enso Relief — acquired by Hinge Health), recovery (RecoverX — acquired by Hyperice), and weight loss (Signos — backed by Dexcom and Google Ventures). This has continued into Fund IV, with our investment in at home blood testing (Rythm Health) and is now continuing in a category seeing unprecedented growth: peptides.

We’re thrilled to announce Courtside’s latest investment in System Labs, which has now raised $20M in new funding led by Patron Fund, with participation from Vine Ventures, Daybreak, SV Angel, Will Ventures, and Courtside.

For the uninitiated, peptides are short chains of amino acids — the same components that assemble into proteins — that function as messengers, instructing cells to repair, regulate, or produce. Your body manufactures them on its own, and since the 1950s we’ve been able to synthesize them in a lab. You’ve almost certainly encountered one without realizing it: insulin is a peptide, and so is every GLP-1 on the market today (the “P” in GLP-1 is literally peptide).

That last point deserves more attention than it gets, because GLP-1s are the most convincing proof of concept a consumer category could ask for. A single molecule that tells the brain it’s full has reordered how the country approaches obesity, driving roughly $79 billion in 2025 sales with forecasts calling for $190 billion by 2035. The more interesting outcome for us isn’t the revenue — it’s the behavior change. Tens of millions of Americans now inject a compound weekly, on a subscription, and think nothing of it. That was an unthinkable consumer habit five years ago.

GLP-1s, though, are one molecule in a very large library. Compounds like BPC-157, sermorelin, NAD+, glutathione, TB-500, and MOTS-c are already being used to accelerate injury recovery, blunt the effects of aging, shift body composition, and improve focus and sleep. Hundreds more have been formulated and thousands sit in development, which is a strange thing to say about a category the average consumer only discovered last year.

But consumers are discovering it, fast. A recent New Consumer × Coefficient Capital survey put familiarity with peptides above 40% among Gen Z and Millennials, a remarkable number for a product category that lived almost entirely in group chats and message boards two years ago. TikTok has crossed 50M posts tagged #peptides. Google searches for the term are at an all-time high, and searches for “where to buy peptides” have climbed more than 500% in the last twelve months.

Which brings us to the problem — and the opportunity.

Peptides have been around for over a decade, but they’ve never had a legitimate front door. Bodybuilders and endurance athletes were ordering CJC-1295 and ipamorelin off unmarked websites throughout the 2010s, with the longevity crowd right behind them. Then in September 2023, the FDA placed a slate of these compounds into its restricted “Category 2” bucket, which stopped licensed compounding pharmacies from preparing them and cited limited human-safety data as the reason.

Demand did not stop. It simply relocated. What followed was a sprawling “research use only” grey market, where sellers shipped vials stamped “Not for human consumption!” to customers who fully intended to consume them. Ingredients were sourced opaquely, testing was uneven to nonexistent, and no clinician was involved anywhere in the process. Despite all of that (and maybe because of it) the grey market grew into an estimated $1–3 billion business.

Two forces are now dismantling that arrangement at the same time, and their combined effect is what makes this moment investable rather than merely interesting.

The first is regulatory. In February 2026, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the broader MAHA effort pushed to reclassify roughly 14 of the 19 compounds the FDA had restricted, reopening a path for licensed U.S. compounding pharmacies to prepare them under a physician’s prescription. This July, the FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee reviewed seven peptides and recommended six of them — BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTS-c, Semax, and Epitalon — for the 503A list. That recommendation isn’t a final rule, and additional committee meetings are scheduled through the coming months. But after years of the door being nailed shut, it is now visibly opening.

The second is enforcement. While the compliant path widens, the illegitimate one is being closed with real urgency. Warning letters went out to research-use-only sellers this past April, and several of the largest grey-market operators have shut down or been raided. Practically speaking, this hands millions of existing, habituated, price-insensitive customers to whoever can serve them legally, transparently, and effectively.

We think that hand-off is worth an enormous amount. The global peptide therapeutic market is already estimated at $140 billion in 2025 and projected to reach $163 billion in 2026 — and the consumer wellness slice of it, still a small fraction of that total, is compounding at better than 50% annually, yielding a ceiling is difficult to overstate. U.S. GLP-1 users roughly doubled from 16M to 32M in eighteen months; apply typical peptide pricing of around $175 a month to a base that size and one compound is already a ~$96 billion market. Extend that to 267M American adults running a protocol or two and the arithmetic runs past $1 trillion.

The conclusion we reached after dozens of conversations with operators, clinicians, and candidly our own firsthand experimentation is that brands are not the scarce asset here. There is no shortage of peptide brands being launched right now. What is much harder to do (and the real opportunity) is building an enterprise scale, regulated infrastructure underneath a peptide brand — and that is precisely what drew us to System.

It is, in other words, the same structural bet we keep making in wellness: own the vertical integration, not just the storefront. System owns all three layers of the peptide business cycle. On the front end, it’s a peptide-first, world-class consumer brand with a clinician in the loop. Underneath sits a 503A compounding pharmacy inside its own network, preparing only regulated, Category 1 peptides (quite different from others selling in the grey market) and serving patients in all 50 states, which moves System from reseller to owner of the supply chain itself. And on top of that, System is building a rapidly growing B2B arm that white-labels the same infrastructure out to clinics, gyms, and other telehealth brands.

This vertical integration is key. System has every product third-party lab tested, runs the compounding through a pharmacy in its own network, and owns the end consumer relationship — which means the answer to “what is actually in this vial, and who is accountable for it” lives inside one company rather than scattered across an anonymous supply chain. On top of that, System is deliberately building an American operation, compounding domestically under U.S. pharmacy licensure and working to bring more of the supply chain onto American soil over time, including a raw-ingredient (API) manufacturer now on its roadmap. In a category where “shipped from overseas, tested by nobody” has been the default, System is bringing “American made” and “100% transparent” to the forefront.

System was founded by Adam Steinle, a highly skilled operator and a strong reason we’re in this deal. Adam has run this exact playbook before, building compliant clinical infrastructure alongside aggressive direct-to-consumer growth at Verse Therapy, scaling it to 100+ providers across 14 states. He’s ex-Facebook and ex-Goldman, and has a track record for scaling this type of model.

Adam has also assembled what we’d argue is the strongest team in the category. The System team brings top-level experience from Joon Health (YC W22), Peloton, TikTok, Scale AI, existing compounding pharmacy operators, and more.

A generational consumer habit has already been established by GLP-1s, years of suppressed demand is being released by regulators, and the illegitimate supply that served that demand is being actively dismantled. We think peptides become one of the defining consumer health categories of this decade, and we couldn’t be more bullish on System’s odds of anchoring it.

New customers can try System at 50% off their first month at systemlabs.com.

item.title: Announcing Courtside x The 4th Quarter
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
When we launched Courtside Ventures in 2016, the prevailing belief in the market was that the only way to make money in sports was through team ownership. Our fund was born out of a very different perspective — shaped by our partner Vasu’s own challenges in raising capital from VCs for his first startup, Krossover.

Nearly a decade later, we’ve raised over $300M, backed founders across 10+ countries, and seen multiple portfolio companies acquired — including exits to Microsoft, The New York Times and Salesforce. Today, as we invest out of our new Fund IV, one thing is clear: while team ownership continues to dominate headlines, the most transformative opportunities in sports lie at the intersection of technology, entertainment, and media.

While the sports industry has grown faster than we ever forecasted, we’ve noticed an unexpected gap in the marketplace — a lack of consistent, in-depth analysis connecting the macro forces shaping the business of sports, entertainment, and technology.

That’s why we’re thrilled to announce Courtside’s The 4th Quarter, a media platform built to explore this intersection with depth, context, and credibility. We are joining forces with the impressive founders of The 4th Quarter, who in a short period of time, have created a strong platform and loyal following by prioritizing unique perspectives.

This collaboration isn’t about competing with existing sports media, who are core to the industry — it’s about complementing them. Our goal is to provide sharp analysis, original reporting, and actionable insights for the founders, operators, and investors shaping the future of this industry.

Together, we’ll deliver:

  • Weekly recaps breaking down the biggest moves across sports, tech, and entertainment
  • Deep-dive features and spotlights on founders, operators and executives
  • Podcasts with industry pioneers
  • Exclusive invite-only events bringing this community together

Courtside brings a unique vantage point as one of the first venture funds solely focused on sports and adjacent categories — from content, collectibles and wellness, to gaming and fan engagement. Partnering with The 4th Quarter — an emerging leader in sports-business storytelling — allows us to pair our industry expertise with The 4th Quarter’s independent editorial voice and growing audience.

You can sign up for Courtside’s The 4th Quarter here.

item.title: Why We Invested: Fanstake
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
As early-stage investors that intentionally emphasize market size, growth rates, and disruption dynamics, we’ve been hard-pressed at Courtside to find a sector within the sports world experiencing more rapid growth and change than NIL in college sports.

Since July 1, 2021 — when the NCAA first allowed college athletes to monetize their name, image, and likeness (“NIL”) — over $2.4 billion has entered the NIL ecosystem in football alone, growing a staggering 43% annually according to Knight-Newhouse. This explosion in athlete funding has had an immediate and obvious impact on collegiate decision making, with 2.3k athletes in men’s basketball entering the transfer portal in 2025 (representing 40% of all players and 11% growth from 2024).

But for all the headlines, hype, opinions, and change, most fans haven’t participated in NIL beyond just reading articles online and hoping that their school of choice is doing its part to stay competitive. With nearly all NIL activity to-date coming from donors, brands, or school-affiliated collectives, NIL has remained an opaque and frustrating topic for the larger population of fans.

This is exactly where Fanstake comes in.

After following the NIL market for years and patiently waiting for the right venture-scale opportunity, we are thrilled to share that Courtside has led Fanstake’s $6.25M Seed round, with participation from Susa Ventures, Will Ventures, Scrum Ventures, Myriad Ventures, Alumni Ventures and others as we back a team we believe is building the future of NIL.

Fanstake is the first fan-powered NIL marketplace and engagement platform. The company allows college sports fans to pledge money to recruit or retain athletes for their favorite teams — but only paying if the athlete commits to their team. As a fully transparent, gamified platform, Fanstake is directly allowing fans to influence the recruiting strategies of their alma maters and programs of choice, all through a fully compliant NIL marketplace.

Founded by Greg Glass, Donnie Flood, and Alex Boisvert, Fanstake is led by a high-powered group of successful former founders with consumer software experience. The team previously built Bizo, a marketing software company acquired by LinkedIn for $175M and have since held senior leadership roles at multiple unicorns including Headspace, Guild, and LinkedIn.

In Fanstake, this team is tackling a rapidly growing category still held back by an inability to meet untapped consumer demand. While top school collectives are spending $14M+ per year on average per Opendorse, the long-tail of 195M collegiate fans (largest fanbase in the US) have been left out of perhaps the biggest recruiting driver in today’s landscape. Fans are clearly willing to support their schools financially as attendance and ticket sales have hit all time highs, but current methods of fan NIL giving facilitated by schools (seat fees, concession surcharges, and athletic fees) have been received poorly, largely seen as pass-through costs with opaque outcomes rather than a tool for fan engagement.

Fanstake flips this dynamic on its head, creating a fully transparent and fan-controlled method for NIL giving via an open-market competition, putting fans in the drivers seat of spend, recruiting strategy, and fanbase engagement, all benefits not available to consumers today.

While individual opinions on the impact of NIL range widely, it is abundantly clear to us at Courtside that the future of college sports involves fair and transparent athlete compensation. While “Phase 1” of this effort occurred in 2021 with the allowance of NIL monetization and “Phase 2” of direct athlete payments is nearly complete with the House Settlement case, we believe that “Phase #3” in NIL is the democratization of athlete compensation beyond just the NCAA, schools, and boosters and instead to the entire fanbase. We believe Fanstake is perfectly positioned to help usher in this new era of NIL monetization at scale.

🔗 Learn more at Fanstake.com

✉️ Interested in talking with the team? We’re happy to connect you.

item.title: Why We Invested: Baller League
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
At Courtside, we’ve been closely tracking a dynamic of two potentially competitive forces in sports content: 1) unprecedented demand for new IP among sports fans and 2) changing consumer viewership preferences seeking short-form experiences.

While equally important and noteworthy in their own right, together, these two trends have had an unexpected impact that we’ve been exploring as we search for investment opportunities best positioned to capitalize on these collective trends.

It is with this backdrop that we are excited to announce our latest investment into one of the most exciting modern sports IP properties we’ve ever come across: Baller League. Founded by media & entertainment executive and pro soccer insider, Felix Starck, Baller League is an emerging league bringing a new era of soccer competition to various parts of the world. Started in Germany and now expanding into the US and UK, the league offers a brand new six-a-side format made for and distributed through streaming platforms such as YouTube, TikTok, and Twitch. Catering to a massive cohort of younger soccer fans globally, the league offers 11 matches over the course of the season, each only 30 minutes long with innovative rules that keep competition and entertainment levels high.

Beyond the innovative structure of the league itself, Baller League’s distribution method is what caught our eye most when evaluating the opportunity. From Day 1, Baller League has attracted key personalities across each of its markets to act as distribution and a driving force behind its free-to-stream offering. In Germany, the league has seen support from former professionals including Luis Figo, John Terry, and dozens more. In conjunction with the league’s US & UK launches (the latter set for March 24th), Baller League has similarly attracted key former professionals, but has also brought in major creators including Olajide Olatunji (known as KSI) and Darren Jason Watkins Jr (known as IShowSpeed), who combine to bring more than 58M YouTube subscribers to the platform.

In a world where younger sports fans are following players and personalities more than leagues and teams, Baller League is tapping into a revolutionary shift in content consumption: using athletes and creators as distribution instead of leaning solely on paid channels. This has led to astounding viewership and Tier 1 sponsorship interest in Seasons 1 & 2 of Germany alone, with similar momentum leading into the US & UK launches in 2025.

There has never been a time in history with greater consumer appetite for sports content than today. In the US, 96M people watched live sports on digital platforms in 2023, marking the first time digital viewership surpassed traditional television engagement. On the international stage, recent worldwide sporting events have reached historic viewership levels, with the ICC Men’s T20 Cricket World Cup attracting 2.6 billion viewers, the 2024 Paris Olympics registering over 3 billion viewers, and the UEFA Euro 2024 tournament in Germany bringing in an astounding 5 billion viewers. This global surge has led to unprecedented growth in the value of sports media rights, which collectively surpassed $60B globally for the first time ever in 2024

In spite of all this growth and demand, the modern world of short-form, hyper-changing content loops are changing the way younger generations consume content…with traditional sports IP largely hamstrung in its ability to adapt. With only 19% of younger fans wanting to watch full sports games, 34% of younger fans preferring highlights over full games, and short-form sports content expected to grow in value by 100% over the next year (faster than the value of live media rights), it’s abundantly clear that younger sports fans are seeking their content in shorter bursts over social media compared to traditional, long-form viewership on television.

While emerging leagues cater perfectly to this phenomenon, not all are created equal. Over the past two years, there has been a notable rise in the formation of emerging leagues, with significant investor interest across the board. We’ve seen multiple examples of leagues pop up recently in fresh categories like golf, snowboarding, sailing, and many more. While we at Courtside we have closely followed all of these launches to date and have made previous league investments in IP such as Drone Racing League (sold to Infinite Reality for $250M), we’ve continued to search for leagues that specifically offer new sports IP but, more importantly, accomplish the rare feat of appealing to traditional sports fans while simultaneously offering modern distribution that caters to a younger demographic hooked on short-form content, something Baller League is tailor-made to accomplish and in our opinion is a perfect fit to succeed as a key sports IP of the future.

item.title: Why We Invested: Eternal
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
You’d be hard pressed to find a consumer trend more talked about in 2024 than wellness and preventative health.

Prevention-based / wellness care, in contrast to traditional / treatment-focused care, has exploded in popularity across the US over the past twelve months. According to Deloitte, prevention-based wellness spend is on pace to surpass traditional care for the first time ever by 2033 (at which time it will be a $3.5T market). With 82% of consumers now considering wellness to be a top priority in their everyday lives, we’ve reached a pivotal shift in the health industry where consumers are allocating outsized wallet share towards wellness.

While wellness as a whole has taken many forms, our team at Courtside has believed that an outsized crossover exists within sports x wellness. Often at the leading edge of health and training innovations, athletes have always emphasized wellness at a higher clip than the greater population, but have often seen solutions come to market that bifurcate their two lives…serving them either as athletes or individuals…but rarely both.

Our latest investment aims to bring these two worlds back together. It is with this backdrop that we are thrilled to announce Courtside’s investment in Eternal, a new healthcare service tailored to lifelong athletes. We are thrilled to co-lead the company’s $13M seed round with Lightspeed Venture Partners, with participation from Founders Fund, Next Ventures, Bling Capital, and more.

Founded by Alex Mather, the former co-founder of The Athletic (Courtside Fund I portfolio company), Eternal aims to keep athletes active, healthy, and performing their best for as long as possible. Offering a membership model, the company combines robust assessments, medical diagnostics, and ongoing guidance and accountability coaching to help athletes optimize performance, address injuries, adapt to hormonal shifts, manage long-term health, and achieve personalized athletic goals well into their later decades.

Part of Eternal’s key value-add is in its sport-based approach. Initially focused on runners, cyclists, and triathletes, the company will offer best-in-class, tailored coaching with expertise on a sport-by-sport basis. Assessments and curriculum for members are curated by some of the top, sport-specific minds in the world including Stacy Sims, (expert in female physiology and nutrition science), Lauren Fleshman (former pro-distance runner and run coach), Andrew Talansky (triathlete, coach, and former pro cyclist), and Rick Celebrini (former pro and head of sports medicine for the Warriors).

Eternal will be opening up its platform (and doors) in San Francisco and New York City in the first half of 2025, and is currently taking on prospective members via its early-access waitlist at eternal.co.

It’s become clear to us at Courtside that while preventative health is the future, functioning health that lets consumers do what they love longer is what is most important. In a recent Consumer Survey that asked whether people would rather live 25% healthier or 25% longer, a clear majority across every generation indicated they’d rather live healthier. Within sports, athletes spend thousands of hours in their first couple decades of life dedicated to their craft in hopes of competing at a high level. While nothing (yet) can truly turn back the clock, we believe that athletes can and should be able to enjoy and compete in sport into their marginal decades as a way to truly live fully fulfilled lives.

We could not be more thrilled to be backing Alex (and team) once again, as we aim to make sports participation a lifelong endeavor.

item.title: Reflecting on The Future of Sports: Thoughts Coming out of The RAISE Global Conference
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
When I tell people that Courtside Ventures invests in sports, they always ask “do you buy stakes in teams?” The answer for us has been the same from the beginning: No.

While franchise values have continued to go up and to the right and ownership groups with liquidity events have seen returns that consistently outperform the stock market, we set out in 2016 to prove that sports, and our constantly-evolving definition of them, represent much more than team ownership. Rather, at Courtside, we’ve closely followed the proliferation of sports on a global scale and have found ourselves investing in the multi-billion dollar verticals surrounding sports that are part of everyday life, including digital media, gaming, collectibles, wellness, and live entertainment.

While investing in these categories (and at the earliest stages) was a novel idea back in 2016, we quickly proved out the venture opportunity with multiple success stories in Fund I. As one of our first investments in sports, Courtside led the Seed round in The Athletic, a subscription-based sports content platform that offers premium coverage of local market teams. We sat on the board from the Seed round until the company was acquired by the New York Times for $550M in cash about 5 years later, returning our entire fund in and of itself. In collectibles, we were one of the first institutional investors into StockX, one of the world’s largest marketplaces for sneaker collectors that furthered the concept of collectibles being an asset class. After a few years involved in the company, we strategically sold 80% of our stake in 2021 at a $7B valuation representing a 99x cash-on-cash return. In gaming, we invested in Beam, an interactive video game streaming platform, which was acquired by Microsoft’s gaming division only nine months after our initial investment. While these three deals reflect a few of the early success stories we’ve seen at Courtside, the growth of sports, gaming, and lifestyle categories at a global level leave us with even deeper conviction on the venture opportunities ahead. As is the case with every fund we have raised, while maintaining a vertical focus, our thesis will change as distribution, society, technology, and trends evolve.

What makes investing in sports so unique at this moment in time? Simply put, sports are embedded in the fabric of global culture, impacting communities of passionate fans, consumers, and collectors on a daily basis. It is clear to me, just by seeing the World Series viewership numbers, that sports have a unique ability to bring people together. As evidenced by Game 2 viewership numbers in Japan, the Shohei Ohtani effect has resulted in unprecedented viewership outside of the US. It is hard to fathom other industries where the eyes of an entire nation are on one man, and a game he is playing for 2 hours at 4am local time. What about another example outside of baseball? Let’s look at the impact of Cricket; the India vs Pakistan T-20 match, played in Long Island this summer, saw some of the highest ticket prices ever recorded — with global viewership of the game surpassing 400M. And if somehow that’s not enough of an example, what about racing or womens sports? F1 continues to capture record audiences and attendance at events, and the rise of women’s sports like WNBA and NWSL have continued to expand the sports audience, and overall team valuations. The best part (to us), is that this is just the beginning.

While impressive across the board among consumer engagement and popularity, the growth of sports has gone far beyond fan metrics and into major B2B and commercial realms. Despite some indicating they would never get involved in live sports, many FANGMA companies have recently bought major sports rights packages — driving team valuations, player salaries, and many downstream business models to unprecedented levels. Recent NFL and NBA media rights deals signed for $100B and $76B respectively have fueled this growth and proven the stickiness and importance of sports viewership to first-time entrants such as Apple, Amazon, and Netflix in their race to grow subscriptions. Beyond large tech players, Private Equity has gotten in on the party too. On the back of record breaking team valuations and continued franchise growth, PE firms were recently approved to buy stakes in NFL teams, further institutionalizing sports as a PE asset class.

In our opinion, it is often overlooked that sports as a category are largely uncorrelated to the pendulum swings of public markets, proving consistent and reliable growth throughout market cycles. At Courtside Ventures, we are constantly seeking unconventional alpha and market leading returns, and the sports category’s unprecedented and unshakable growth has proven to yield unique alpha for our LPs by providing exposure to the business models, early trends, and emerging geographies we invest in. While not every one of our investments may be uncorrelated to the public markets, our portfolios as a whole provide global exposure to the best founders building in sports or the surrounding markets that are expected to grow to $630B by 2028.

To me, sports have impacted my life immeasurably, and I love what I do. Something I’ve learned through my love of sports is that they represent one of the last parts of humanity that bring us together. When I go to a stadium, every age, gender, race, religion and even political party comes together to cheer on a group of players for a common cause. People travel from around the world or tune in globally to watch the drama play out. Sports are played in war time and in peace. Sports provide joy, serendipity, spontaneity, and escape at a level unmatched by any other form of entertainment. “It’s why you play the game!” — watching the underdog pull out a win. Sorry to all the Bears fans reading this post, but the recent Hail Mary that was executed by the Commander’s is the exact reason you play to the last whistle, a glimmer of hope that allows you to erupt in either the thrill of victory or the agony of defeat. Sports were here long before any of us were around and will be here when we are all long gone.

Almost everything I learned about being successful in my career has come from lessons learned in sports; hard work, perseverance, team work, dedication, determination, discipline … and most importantly, a desire to improve every time I stepped on the field. But not everyone who bench presses 400 pounds or runs a 4.3 40 yard dash ends up being the best player. In sports, your instinct or “basketball IQ” sometimes allows undersized, less athletic players to thrive at a top level. My work in venture has been a combination of hard work, apprenticeship, constant reps, and a desire to get better every year, coupled with an instinct in and around the world of sports, gaming, and entertainment.

One question I was asked at the Raise Global conference was, “How do you see around corners?” The simple answer is, you can’t, but if the sun is shining in the right direction, you can see a shadow. If the wind is blowing in the direction, you can get a sniff of what is coming. If you listen closely enough, you can hear footsteps approaching. Venture is a combination of hard work, intelligence, skill, timing, and instinct. Of course, we all have to focus on large markets, great founders, and operational excellence of startups. But as is true in the world of sports, it is also true in venture — you need a little bit of luck to be on top no matter how good you are. I believe that in life and in work, you make your luck through hard work, discipline, and determination. We are lucky to have already driven great returns for our investors and hope to continue to do the same moving forward in future funds.

item.title: Courtside Ventures — By the Numbers
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
Courtside Ventures — By the Numbers

When we started Courtside in 2016, we did so out of desperate market need. Not only was there no venture fund that focused on sports, but existing VCs would run to the hills every time they saw a sports deal. This left entrepreneurs constantly having to look for alternate sources of funding, mostly from the very people that we call LPs today. Fast forward 7 years, and through 3 early stage funds, over 100 investments, and $200M+ in AUM, Courtside has proved the thesis that venture returns can be achieved in sports and associated categories. While Fund III is still in its infancy, we thought it made sense to share our learnings from Fund I and Fund II, which we hope will not only bring more venture dollars into the sports, gaming, and lifestyle ecosystems, but also help entrepreneurs understand the economics of venture scale businesses.

Fund I

In 2016, Courtside Fund I was launched as a $35M vehicle backed by just 2 LPs. If only fundraising was that simple today! In every sense of the phrase, Fund I was very much a “proof of concept” fund. We needed to not only show that there were enough quality deals in our area of focus, but also that we could win them, and generate sizable enough returns to compete against the general venture capital space. In total, we made 41 investments out of Fund I, but in hindsight thought that we had probably made 6–8 more investments than we should have (lesson #1 as first time fund managers).

Our average initial check into a company out of this fund was $359K and our largest overall position in any company was $5.6M across 3 checks. Out of 41 investments, 9 have exited in some sort of net positive outcome, 18 are dead, and 14 are still active. The 9 exits in aggregate allowed us to generate a 1.7X DPI to LPs in 5 years, although almost all of that came from just 2 deals, and we recycled the proceeds from the other 7 smaller exits. The value of the 15 remaining positions today is ~$28.7M, which if we were to add to the ~$60.3M we have generated in proceeds already, gives us a MOIC / TVPI of 2.83x / 2.46x respectively.

In order to do 41 deals over the course of ~3 years, we looked at ~6000 deals. That’s about a 0.6% success rate. To put that in perspective, Harvard’s acceptance rate is about 3.6%. What’s truly amazing about venture is that even after being so selective, less than 10% of a fund’s portfolio drives nearly all of the returns, and this seems to hold true for a thesis driven thematic fund as much as it does for a generalist fund. Two deals thus far have generated almost all our returns to date, and differ wildly from each other in scope and investment size. In “Deal #1”, we led the Seed and Series A rounds, reinvested in the Series B, and sat on the company’s board until exit. In aggregate we invested $5.6M and generated ~$31.2M in proceeds. In “Deal #2”, we invested $200K in the Seed round and another $117K in the Series A, yielding a total investment of $317K, ultimately selling 80% of our stake in a secondary transaction and returning ~$29.7M of proceeds. Wildly different paths to similar outcomes!

Fund II

On the back of Fund I’s success, we raised Fund II in 2019 as a $54M vehicle, with significantly more than 2 LPs. Seeing the increasing crossover of sports and gaming, we added a third partner who exclusively focused on gaming investments. Having learned our portfolio construction lesson from Fund I, we knew we wanted to have greater conviction in each deal, thus writing bigger checks and taking larger ownership stakes. As such, in Fund II, we made 30 investments with an average check size of $763k, with our largest position in a company totaling $5.5M. Out of the 30 investments, 3 were acquired, 7 are dead, and 20 are still active. None of the 3 acquisitions returned any meaningful capital, but the 21 active companies are currently valued at ~$106M, giving us an MOIC and TVPI of 2.34x and 2.02x respectively. Once again, showing the power law of venture, 70% of that value comes from just 2 companies, and 91% of it comes from 6 companies. Given the larger fund size and our focus on making higher conviction bets, our winning deals in Fund II look a little more alike than in Fund I. In “Deal #1”, we initially invested $3M, followed by an additional $2.4M in a subsequent round. The company is wildly profitable, hasn’t had to raise any money for the past 2 years, and our holdings are currently valued at ~$38M. In “Deal #2”, we led the Seed round with a $2M check and then invested another $1.6M in a subsequent round. This company is doing north of $50M in revenue and our stake is currently valued at ~$33M. Unlike in Fund I, we see at least 3 other companies that currently have line of sight to being fund returners, given our ownership and their traction. Similar to Fund I though, we looked at over 6000 companies in aggregate in order to do 30 deals, dropping our success rate to 0.5%.

Fund III

In 2021 we raised Fund III, which was a $100M fund. It’s still too early to share any metrics or learnings from this fund, but we will likely end up with about 34 investments, with an average check size of $1.5M. Our largest initial check to date has been $4.0M and 35% of our deals were based outside the US, with a specific focus on gaming in emerging markets such as India, Latin America and parts of Africa. We look forward to having (hopefully positive) numbers to share in a few years time.

7 years ago, conventional wisdom in the venture world was that you couldn’t generate outsized returns in sports. Part of that was certainly a myopic view of the industry being products that were sold to sports teams and athletes. Today, everyone knows that sports is so much more than just that. It encompasses the world of media, fantasy, betting, gaming, wellness and collectibles. There have already been numerous billion dollar plus companies created across these verticals, and we have no doubt that there will continue to be large outcomes in the years to come. We look forward to being in the Seed round of as many of those unicorns as possible!

item.title: Why We Invested: Camb AI
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
Consumer thirst for content seems unquenchable these days. Globally, the average person spends 6 hours and 37 minutes each day on screens according to DataReportal, consuming content across a variety of mediums including social media, television, web, audio, short-form, long-form, and everything in-between. It’s probably no surprise that Americans consume more content than the average person globally (6 hours and 59 minutes), but many large countries internationally actually far exceed the US’s digital consumption. In Mexico, the average person spends just over 8 hours a day on screens. In Argentina, screen time takes up 9 hours per day. And in Brazil and South America, over 9.3 hours a day are spent digitally.

In fact, international demand for various forms of content is growing faster than in the US, as tech adoption and internet access continue to break through to a greater portion of the world. In 2023, Netflix saw non-English stories make up 30% of all viewing. In the world of sports, where media rights reached an all-time high of $55B in 2023 (per Citizen Gaming Group), multiple leagues are strategically looking internationally for fan and audience growth. The NBA in particular expects fans from over 200 countries to tune into games during the 2023 / 2024 season, with approximately 10% of all team and league revenue generated outside of the US per CNBC.

All-in-all, content of various forms is seeing global explosion, which has created a need and opportunity for globally relevant properties which can cross local language barriers. MrBeast was one of the best examples of this. As the biggest individual YouTuber in the world with over 237M subscribers on his English channel, MrBeast now owns the biggest channel in 7 different countries, which is mainly attributed to his early adoption of multi-lingual videos. Though a key driver to his success, the ability to translate content historically has not been possible for the wider market due to accuracy, costs, or time it took to translate content.

It’s for these reasons why we are excited to announce our latest investment into Camb AI, an AI-powered language translation service building a platform of tools to help creators, rights holders, and other content providers generate instantaneous, hyper-realistic translations and content localization at a fraction of the cost of alternative services. Courtside led the company’s $4M Seed round, which included other investors such as DFDF, TRTL Ventures, Blue Star Innovation Partners, and others.

Based in Dubai, Camb was founded by Avneesh Prakash (CEO) and Akshat Prakash (CTO), alongside a team that brings Generative AI and Machine Learning experience from Carnegie Mellon, Apple, and Amazon. Camb AI’s proprietary MARS and BOLI technology allows the platform to learn a speaker’s unique voice intonations and inflections with only a few seconds of audio, allowing for the translation of content in near-real time to over 120 different languages. While translation is a key part of Camb’s offering, we were especially drawn to the company’s ability to maintain a speaker’s voice, while also dissecting and accounting for colloquial language. In media, sports, and creator-driven content, authentic and accurate translations that can pick up on local dialect differences create better consumer experiences and more loyal audiences, and Camb’s offering is unrivaled in its ability to capture this translation nuance.

The company’s technology has already seen adoption across a multitude of content formats. Camb has worked with many mega-influencers who are looking to internationalize their audiences, partnering with creators such as BeerBiceps, Nick DiGiovanni, and Narin’s Beauty to translate videos that have generated over 250M+ views. In media, Camb has worked directly with production teams, most recently translating the world’s first fully AI-dubbed multilingual feature film for Nayla Al Khaja’s horror film Three, which was first shown at the Red Sea Festival in Saudi Arabia in late 2023. In sports, Camb was recently selected by Major League Soccer to join into the league’s first-ever cohort for its MLS Innovation Lab. Additionally, the company was selected for the 2024 AO Startups Program, a JV between Tennis Australia, Wildcard Ventures, and Techstars where Camb’s technology was recently used to provide AI-based translation to the 2024 Australian Open.

At Courtside, we’ve closely followed the globalization of the Sports, Gaming, and Lifestyle categories across our three funds dating back to 2016. With approximately 20% of our investments being made outside of the US, we’ve taken a worldwide approach to consumer trends, and have seen content consumption (namely in sports and media) explode internationally. After spending time getting to know the Camb team, technology, and problem set they aim to tackle, we think the company has a unique opportunity to become the localization infrastructure of the future, specifically in the way consumers engage with sports and media. As Generative AI technology continues to rapidly improve, and Camb’s proprietary platform nears fully-live translation, we look forward to a future where sports fans across the globe can tune into any game in their local language and enjoy the excitement that comes from experiencing live sports coverage. In the meantime, we are excited to support Camb and the company’s mission to make various forms of content available to anyone in the world, in the highest quality possible.

item.title: Why We Invested: Commons Clinic
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
Musculoskeletal (MSK) disorders, especially those related to sports injuries or sports-related damage, have long been an issue across all ages of athletes and competitors. According to the National Safety Council, in the United States alone, there were over 314,000 basketball injuries, 265,000 football injuries, and over 179,000 soccer injuries treated in emergency rooms in 2022, with far more never resulting in immediate hospital visits, potentially leading to worsened injuries in the future.

All these issues result in a massive amount of health-related spend falling on both individuals and insurers. The New York Times estimated that the annual financial impact of sports injuries in high-school and college athletes totaled $30 billion. Amongst casual competitors, the Sports & Fitness Industry Association estimated that pickleball alone is expected to contribute upwards of $500 million in healthcare costs this year in the US. Despite improvements in equipment and training, the growth of sports participation at all ages, and the increasing cost of traditional healthcare continue to create a massive financial burden associated with sports injuries and overall MSK care.

When looking beyond just sports injuries, MSK care has ballooned to be one of the biggest sources of health expenditure in the United States, totaling $184B in treatment costs in 2023. This doesn’t include the $34B spent on physical therapy, where MSK patients deal with disjointed health services that don’t talk to each other, being sent off after an operation and often not speaking with their surgeon thereafter to check in on rehab. MSK injury treatment is massively needed, but is currently served by an expensive, complex, and broken health system.

It is with this issue in mind that Courtside is thrilled to announce our investment in Commons Clinic: a full-service, value-based healthcare platform that is pioneering a new way of specialty care in the MSK space. Led by CEO Nick Aubin, Commons Clinic raised $19.5M in Series A funding from investors including Courtside Ventures, RA Capital Management, Floating Point, Time BioVentures, and others. Courtside also previously participated in a prior round for Commons Clinic, as the company has raised over $33M of capital in aggregate.

Commons Clinic’s end-to-end platform provides an alternative to traditional, hospital-based orthopedic and sports injury care. Compared to low-touch, expensive, and often unnecessary surgeries and in-patient treatment, Commons Clinic takes a holistic approach to MSK intervention.

Utilizing its in-house team of top orthopedic physicians, branded care centers, best-in-class surgical facilities, and its virtual clinic offered via mobile-app, Commons Clinic manages the entire care experience for its patients. This vertically-integrated platform and value-based model allows Commons to provide upfront, bundled pricing options to patients, yielding simple and transparent care processes not seen in traditional (non value-based) healthcare where patients are billed after the fact and oftentimes have no idea how much they will owe. Additionally, by managing a patient’s entire care experience from start to finish, Commons Clinic connects physicians with physical therapists, allowing for complete communication amongst all parties and greater adherence to physical therapy and other non-surgical rehab options. The company utilizes a network of ambulatory surgery centers to conduct necessary outpatient procedures, saving an average of 40% in costs compared to traditional, hospital-based procedures.

Commons Clinic currently operates in the Los Angeles market, with its footprint including six top-tier surgeons, three clinics, and a top five national health plan as its anchor value-based partner. With this funding, Commons aims to continue its expansion across Southern California, with hopes to enter additional markets across the US in the future.

Though not traditional healthcare investors, Courtside has long explored the intersection of sports, fitness, and longevity, recognizing the ongoing challenge that injuries and the traditional methods for treatment / rehab have brought about for both the professional and casual athlete as well as the general population. Given our close relationships across professional sports, we have also seen how teams and leagues share this area of focus, with a growing number of them directly partnering with local hospitals or healthcare practices either through naming rights, sponsorship deals, or other means of collaboration. We believe that Commons Clinic’s model of partnering physicians and physical therapists with a technology enabled, low-cost platform has the potential to create valuable improvements in the MSK space, benefiting both the professional athlete suffering from a torn ACL as well as an elderly person dealing with joint pain.

We are excited about Commons Clinic’s approach to injury treatment and rehab, as well as the significant savings it yields for both consumers and the healthcare system as a whole. As pro teams, college programs, and youth leagues continue to invest in injury technology, we think Commons Clinic is well positioned to be the provider of choice for the next iteration of injury treatment for athletes and the general population. We couldn’t be more thrilled to be partnering with Commons Clinic and hope to help the company continue transforming the MSK and sports injury market.

item.title: Why We Invested: EloElo
item.dc:creator: Courtside Ventures
item.content:encoded:
The Indian gaming industry is exploding, no matter how you look at it.

As the most populous country in the world, India currently has 500M gamers (casual and competitive) growing 12% annually, and a total market that is expected to surpass $8.7B by 2027. India’s proportion of New Paying Users (NPUs) is growing at the fastest rate of any country in the world: rising from 40% in 2020 to 50% in 2021, and transaction-based games in India saw revenue increases of 26% on average during the year.

India’s macroeconomic conditions are also adding fuel to this gaming trend. In the last five years, disposable income has increased ~45% per capita. At the same time, access to reliable internet and mobile phones has risen rapidly and has been supported by the cheapest data rates in the world ($0.1/GB).

The unprecedented surge in Indian gamers, willingness to pay for games, and underlying macroeconomic tailwinds have all contributed to industry growth that is unrivaled by many other markets and geographies in the world.

It is for these reasons that Courtside has looked to India as a key area of focus and why we are thrilled to announce our investment in Eloelo, the #1 live social gaming and entertainment app in India. Courtside led the company’s Series A round alongside Griffin Gaming Partners.

From the moment we met the team, it was clear to us that Eloelo is pioneering a new form of entertainment in India. Eloelo brings together a unique combination of live streaming, social gaming, and creator-hosted events in a viral gaming app suited perfectly for local Indian culture. By offering a suite of easy-to-play games, advanced creator tools for live streaming, and an overall app design that prioritizes community, the platform has seen unrivaled growth within the Indian social gaming landscape.

With over 40M community members playing games together while live streaming, Eloelo fit our long-held investment thesis perfectly. As previously written about back in 2020, Courtside has firmly believed that the next generation of social networks would revolve around games. As the proliferation of mobile phones, affordability of high speed data plans, and popularity of gaming has bolstered the Indian entertainment ecosystem, Eloelo is well positioned to benefit from these tailwinds and become the next major social media app built via gaming.

While our investment in Eloelo enters a new class of social gaming via live-streaming, it isn’t our first foray into India. Courtside began to identify India as a market of interest for sports and gaming in 2019. We made our first investment in WinZO in Q3 of 2020 and have completed all 6 of our investments in the country within the last 3 years. Given the aforementioned population growth and overall GDP growth in the region, we have taken a diversified approach to portfolio construction in the India gaming ecosystem. Courtside’s investments include real-money gaming, social gaming, sports (cricket), gamified investing, interactive social networking, and web3. These include WinZO — Real-Money Gaming Platform, FanCraze — Sports and Collectibles, Totality Corp — Social Gaming Experiences, IndiGG — Publishing Platform, and Fello — Gamified Savings.

With our most recent investment in Eloelo, Courtside will continue to partner with exceptional founders and funds in India backing the next generation of sports and gaming companies. We are incredibly excited about the future of gaming in India and the diversity of opportunities ahead.
